items.title: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
items.standfirst: Beijing warned that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs.
items.content: U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025. —Brendan Smialowski—Getty ImagesChina warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs, which have reignited global trade tensions.“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.” The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.” Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are. Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”Brazil fights back after being singled outAlongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year. “The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.” Democratic lawmaker vows to tackle Trump’s tariffsThe Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement. “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

items.title: Trump Administration Unveils New Tariffs for China, the European Union, and More
items.standfirst: The Trump Administration proposed sweeping new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, threatening to reignite global tensions.
items.content: President Donald Trump holds up a chart while speaking during a “Make America Wealthy Again” trade announcement event in the Rose Garden at the White House on April 2, 2025. —Chip Somodevilla––Getty ImagesThe Trump Administration on Wednesday proposed sweeping new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union, threatening to reignite global trade tensions.China is set to be hit with the highest rate, facing tariffs of up to 20% on most covered goods. The rate could potentially rise to 40% if Beijing fails to honor the trade truce agreed upon between Beijing and Washington last year.The European Union also faces a proposed tariff rate of 15%, accounting for certain existing duties, which could rise to 20% if existing trade agreements are not honored.The proposed tariffs follow an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s office into what it described as unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity that have placed American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The levies are meant to discourage excess capacity and production in sectors that “are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.”A spokesperson for the European Commission told TIME it will “study the findings” of the report shared by the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), but pushed back against any suggestion of Europe’s contribution to excess manufacturing. “We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” the spokesperson said. “The E.U. and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action.”The European Commission will continue engaging with the U.S. Administration on the implementation of the joint trade agreement signed August 2025, the spokesperson said. “Under the Joint Statement, the 15% all-inclusive ceiling applies to E.U. goods. We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties,” they added.The U.S. tariffs also target other major economies, including key allies Japan and South Korea, which face rates of up to 15%. India, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, Taiwan, and Bangladesh are also included in the sweeping tariffs unveiled on Thanksgiving eve. The levies for these countries remain between 15% to upwards of 25%, with the notable exception of Vietnam, which may face tariffs of up to 35%. Further determinations concerning Mexico and Norway are still being considered.The Trump Administration also announced a separate proposal seeking to increase tariffs on Brazil, targeting the country's sugar and aircraft exports.Read More: Why the Trump Administration Is Being Accused of Interfering in Brazil's ElectionThe Trump Administration said it would impose the tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the government to investigate unfair trade practices abroad and impose tariffs via the executive branch through its findings. The Administration previously announced two investigations in March as it sought ways to revive the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court in February. “The 301 is a very powerful tool, empowering the executive branch to act against other countries when they find something that can arguably be described as an unreasonable discriminatory burden and restrict U.S. commerce,” Kathleen Clausen, a professor at Georgetown Law, tells TIME. She points to the fact that there have already been seven investigations by the USTR under the second Trump Administration, while there were only three during former President Joe Biden’s term.Despite the sweeping proposals, Greer played down concerns that the new tariffs could disrupt the global economy.“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this—they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”The earliest the Administration expects the tariffs to take effect is January 2027, with the proposals first subject to a public comment process and hearings. Any “interested persons” have until Jan. 5, 2027, to submit written comments or requests to appear at the hearings, alongside a summary of their proposed testimony.Anyone can theoretically submit a request for a hearing or a written comment, says Clausen. “Businesses and related workers' groups that are principally affected by these actions are the type of expertise and constituency that would typically be invited to provide oral testimony at the hearing.” In those instances, “by law, the USTR must respond to the comment, not individually, but en masse, where they must address those comments in their determination.”However, she notes that even if there is strong opposition amongst these consultations that may not deter the office of the USTR to go ahead with the implementation of these tariffs.Beijing, ahead of the announcement, reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and dismissed allegations that it was contributing to global manufacturing overcapacity."The so-called 'overcapacity' is ​a ⁠false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world's two largest economies to maintain stable relations.“A way of seeing what happened today is that this is a way to put pressure on our trading partners to be tougher on China,” argues Clausen.“The USTR's feeling is that trading partners have not come to the table prepared to take enough action to combat these problems, either their own or directly with China over the years, and so stronger action was needed to be taken,” she says.The latest tariff proposals, with their heightened focus on China, come just days after Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping struck a friendly tone during the President's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The two leaders joined Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic trilateral sit-down. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in December, when Trump hosts world leaders in Miami for the G20 summit. Clausen points out that under Section 301, the U.S. government must request a consultation with other foreign governments where these tariffs could be used as a bargaining chip in future trade negotiations.“This is an effective time for the Administration if it wants to try and get a deal with these partners in an upcoming meeting when they're together,” she says. “We're in this period of feedback on whether these rates are the right rates for these particular countries, but whether these tariffs materialize, and what kind of exceptions will be built in, remains to be seen.”Trump reignites global tensions with renewed tariffs pushUpon returning to the White House, Trump used tariffs as a hallmark of his protectionist agenda with the announcement of “Liberation Day” in April 2025 which saw a wide-range of sweeping tariffs on major global economies.Although in February the Supreme Court struck down these tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, it set the tone for the types of economic policy the second Trump Administration sought to pursue. Trump has also sought to use tariffs as a tool of economic pressure during trade negotiations. He notably threatened Europe with levies of 50% in May 2025, before reaching a joint agreement the following month that concluded with a 15% tariff ceiling for most E.U. exports.Most recently, following a breakdown in negotiations with Canada, the U.S. introduced 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, which Canada then reciprocated. The countries remain engaged in a contentious trade war with no clear path to a deal.The President has also taken to utilizing tariffs to pursue other policy objectives. In January, he threatened to tariff U.S. allies if they didn’t support his push to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland. The annexation row was settled in September when Denmark, the U.S., and Greenland signed a security deal, expanding U.S. military access to the semi-autonomous territory, without compromising its sovereignty. While the Trump Administration favors tariffs, the practice remains deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the Republicans’ major losses in the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

items.title: Artists and Fans Pay Tribute to Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor
items.standfirst: The Duran Duran guitarist died at age 65 after battling stage 4 prostate cancer, his family and band announced Wednesday.
items.content: Andy Taylor poses with guitars in Maison Rouge Studios in London, U.K., in July 1984.Fans and fellow artists are paying tribute to Andy Taylor, the guitarist of Duran Duran and a Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductee, after his death this week at age 65.Taylor died Monday after a yearslong battle with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. In a joint statement on Wednesday, Taylor’s family and the band said he “passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family.”“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” Duran Duran said. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”Taylor joined the English New Wave band in 1980 when he responded to an ad in bygone British music magazine Melody Maker for a “live-wire guitarist.” At the audition in Birmingham, he met keyboardist Nick Rhodes, bassist John Taylor, and drummer Roger Taylor. (The three Taylors were unrelated.) Later, he met Simon Le Bon, who became the band’s frontman.John Taylor described Andy Taylor in the statement announcing his passing as “a killer riff-merchant, melodist, six string textualist (he would hate that term) and a singer with a great voice. What he brought down to Birmingham on that train from Whitley Bay can never be quantified.”The band released their self-titled debut album in 1981. It was an immediate commercial breakthrough, reaching No. 3 on U.K. charts and the top 10 in Portugal, New Zealand, Sweden, and Australia. It included the songs “Planet Earth” and “Girls on Film.” The album climbed the charts in the U.S. two years later after the success of Duran Duran’s second album Rio.Taylor brought a traditional rock edge to Duran Duran’s New Romantic disco sound, which music critic Alexis Petridis wrote “gave Duran Duran a peculiar commercial edge, particularly in the U.S., a country that had failed to really take to punk or glam rock, and viewed disco as an aberration best forgotten.” Taylor co-wrote some of the band’s greatest hits, including “Hungry Like the Wolf” and “Rio,” and his distorted guitar became a quintessential sound of their music.Much of that influence came from Taylor’s love of AC/DC, Van Halen, and other hard rock bands, some of whose songs he covered in his later solo work. He learned guitar as a teenager from Dave Black, who joined Spiders From Mars after the band parted ways with David Bowie. Taylor left school early, playing at working men’s clubs in northeast England and touring with a cover band at U.S. air bases in West Germany.“I have in my mind the blond bombshell, firebrand teenager I met in 1980,” Le Bon said in his tribute to Taylor. “He’s the kid from the Northeast who can really play guitar. If you like, he can play it like Mick Ronson, or he can play it like Jimmy Paige, he can even play rinky-dink rhythm like Nile Rodgers. But what he does most is play guitar like guitar-genius - Andy Taylor!”“Spikey hair & spikey personality. Andy didn’t mince his words; he didn’t suffer fools gladly. Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short,” Le Bon added.Duran Duran members John Taylor, Roger Taylor, Andy Taylor, Simon Le Bon, and Nick Rhodes on the Shinkansen train in Kyoto, Japan, in April 1982. —Koh Hasebe—Shinko Music/Getty ImagesTaylor formed the British-American supergroup The Power Station with English musician Robert Palmer, former Chic drummer Tony Thompson, and John Taylor in 1984. He left Duran Duran in 1986 to pursue a solo career, telling the Los Angeles Times that he wanted to play rock ’n’ roll while the band was moving towards dance music. He went on to release four solo albums, with the last in 2024.The classic “Fab Five” lineup reunited in 2001, releasing Astronaut in 2004 and playing reunion shows through 2006. Taylor also played on the band’s most recent studio album Danse Macabre in 2023 and its re-recording of “Shadows on Your Side” in 2025.“It was great to make music with him again when the original five reunited in the early 2000s, and that time together, both on stage and in the studio, meant a tremendous amount to all of us,” the band said.The band was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, but by that point Taylor was being treated for prostate cancer and was unable to appear on stage. Instead, Le Bon read an open letter from Taylor that announced his diagnosis.“I’m truly sorry and massively disappointed I couldn’t make it,” the letter read. “Let there be no doubt I was stoked about the whole thing, even bought a new guitar with the essential whammy! I’m so very proud of these four brothers; I’m amazed at their durability, and I’m overjoyed at accepting this award. I often doubted the day would come. I’m sure as hell glad I’m around to see the day.”Inductees Nick Rhodes, John Taylor, Roger Taylor and Simon Le Bon of Duran Duran speak onstage during the 37th Annual Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony in Los Angeles on Nov. 5, 2022. —Theo Wargo—Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of FameThe son of a fisherman, Taylor was born in Tynemouth in Northumberland in 1961 and grew up in the coastal fishing village of Cullercoats. His mother left the family when he was 11 on his first day of secondary school, according to Taylor’s 2008 memoir. Taylor’s devotion to his wife Tracey Wilson, their four children, Georgina, Isabella, Bethany, and Andrew, and his grandson Albie was a common refrain of tributes after his death.“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather. He was the rock of our family,” Taylor’s family said. “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”Taylor met Wilson in 1981 at the Rum Runner club in Birmingham, where Duran Duran was performing. It was Wilson’s 20th birthday. The pair married in 1982. In an interview with People in 2023, Taylor called Wilson his wife of “40,000 years.”Andy Taylor with his wife Tracy and their dog Charlie at home in The Midlands, U.K., in 1982. —John Randle—Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesAmanda Kyme, a celebrity relations manager and the former girlfriend of John Taylor, shared a photo of Andy and his wife. “I took this photo ( amongst many ) of Andy and his beloved wife and beautiful friend Tracey many years ago in Sydney . It’s such a lovely and loving moment I captured between them,” she wrote. “I have so many lovely memories from travelling all over the world with Duran Duran so many pictures of fantastic days &fun times. Rest in peace Andy and I’m thinking of you and the family.”https://www.instagram.com/p/DgLn0mgRwLl/Across his career, Taylor worked as a guitarist, songwriter, and producer for artists like Mark Shaw, Sir Rod Stewart, and Belinda Carlisle.“I’m deeply, deeply saddened to hear of the passing of my dear friend and musical collaborator Andy Taylor. I’m proud to have known and worked with him and he remains one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I’ve ever heard and had the privilege to work with,” Shaw posted on Facebook on Wednesday night. Taylor collaborated with Shaw, vocalist of Then Jerico, on several songs, including “Under Your Spell,” “Love So Bright,” and “Some People.”“His contribution to contemporary music is outstanding and will never be forgotten, like the man himself - ￼ true family man and a generous and loving friend and one of the best guitarists that ever graced God’s Earth,” Shaw added.Stewart shared a photo of Taylor on social media with the caption, “Good bye Andy my dear pal. We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun.” Taylor co-wrote five songs for Stewart’s 1988 album Out of Order.“I was blessed to work with Andy Taylor - such a genius,” Carlisle posted on social media early Thursday. Taylor played the guitar solo in Carlisle’s 1986 song “Mad About You” and appeared in its music video.“Thank you Andy Taylor for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever,” Carlisle added. “I hope you are feeling the love…Godspeed.”David Ellefson, former bassist and backing vocalist for heavy metal band Megadeth, recalled working with Taylor in the early 2000s when Ellefson was an artist relations representative for Peavey Electronics. “I remember going down to the Celebrity Theatre in Phoenix to meet with him and his guitar tech to talk gear and shop,” Ellefson posted on Instagram. “He was a real rocker with a genuine rock ’n’ roll attitude!”“It’s safe to say Duran Duran were one of the greatest pop-rock bands to help define the MTV generation and were stalwarts on Capitol Records during my years there with Megadeth,” Ellefson added. “A real loss for us all. Let’s crank his music loud and celebrate everything he gave us over four decades of incredible music and creative exploration!”The Ting Tings, an English indie pop duo consisting of Katie White and Jules De Martino, posted on social media, “Our dear friend, a true talent and after much time locked in a studio together someone we will never forget. He ran deep.” Taylor co-produced The Ting Tings’ third studio album, Super Critical, in 2014.“A pleasure to spend time in his studio for months on end dreaming up songs and giggling like children when we found one. So much love. We will never forget you,” the duo wrote.Ricky Warwick, lead singer of Thin Lizzy and frontman of Scottish hard rock band The Almighty, posted on Facebook, “I’m going to miss my mate Andy Taylor. It’s hard to take in that I can’t just pick up the phone and hear his voice again and talk all things rock n roll. A phenomenal musician who I had the honor of working with, an even more phenomenal human being, Father and Grandfather.I’m glad I got to know him, and I wish we’d had more time.”Warwick co-wrote “Love or Liberation,” the single that marked Taylor’s return as a solo artist after 13 years. He also collaborated on songs for Taylor’s 2023 album Man’s a Wolf to Man, his first solo album in 33 years. Taylor produced The Almighty’s 1991 album Soul Destruction.Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant posted, “A tough fighter, Andy Taylor … condolences to his tribe.” Plant performed Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven” with Taylor at a cancer benefit Taylor organized in 2023. It was the first time Plant had sung it live since the band’s reunion in 2007 and Taylor’s last documented appearance onstage.In a 2023 interview published Wednesday, Taylor, already five years deep into his battle with cancer, was in the middle of rehearsing for the benefit. “I’m standing here with my fingers bleeding and my throat’s a bit hoarse from singing,” he said, “and I’m very happy about that.”Andy Taylor arrives at Wogan House in central London to appear on the Zoe Ball Breakfast Show on Radio 2 on Aug. 30, 2023. —James Manning—PA Images/Getty ImagesIn late 2022, Le Bon and his wife brought Taylor’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame trophy to his studio in Ibiza. On his way out, Taylor recalled Le Bon asking, “Do you reckon I could come back here and work?” A few months later, Le Bon returned with producer Joshua Blair and a batch of songs for Danse Macabre.Le Bon recalled on Wednesday spending “happy days at the studio in his Ibiza villa, laying down tracks for our latest records,” alongside his memories of their time together “on tour, in the studio, in our little flat on Caroline Road, Balsall Heath at 6am.”“There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart,” Le Bon wrote. “It’ll never close up; I won’t let it.”

items.title: Trump Urges Putin to ‘Pull Back’ Military Aggression in Europe
items.standfirst: The U.S. President expressed hope that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine "quickly" to avoid expansion of the war.
items.content: Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Alaska on Aug. 15, 2025. —Andrew Harnik—Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Thursday said he would like to see Russian President Vladimir Putin “pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe” in the hope that a deal can be made to end the Russia-Ukraine war."During my conversations in ​China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I ⁠spent a lot of time talking about the ​fact that I would like to see President ​Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” said Trump, referencing the meetings he had with Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit last week.Expressing his belief that a deal can be made "quickly," Trump continued: “I really believe this is a strong possibility. Thousands of people are being killed each and every month. A complete bloodbath.”The U.S. President didn’t specify what he meant by “territories throughout Europe,” but his remarks come amid concerns over the possible expansion of the Russia-Ukraine war. A number of recent incidents involving NATO members have sparked fears. Last week, Poland accused Russia of ⁠violating its airspace after two missiles and a drone crashed in its territory. Russia denied violating Poland’s airspace. Estonia also recently accused Russian security services ​of ordering an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defense company. Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the accusation “unfounded,” denying Moscow’s involvement. Tensions escalated further this week when Russia alleged that Estonia was quietly allowing Ukrainian drones to use its airspace to strike northwestern Russia and accused Tallinn of trying to obstruct Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea. Estonia vehemently denied both accusations calling them “baseless,” with Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stressing that the country “has not allowed and will not allow its territory or airspace to be used for drone attacks against Russia from Ukraine.”Trump’s update came a day after he met with NATO chief Mark Rutte at his Mar-a-Lago estate. Trump said he informed Rutte of his conversations with Putin during the meeting, which primarily focused on Ukraine and Iran.In a joint statement issued Wednesday night, Trump and Rutte said the “impactful” sit-down had seen them discuss the “importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible.”Offering his own reflections of the meeting, Rutte—who has previously been dubbed the “Trump whisperer”—said: “It’s clearer than ever that American leadership remains essential as we build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.” U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resumed earlier this month after a nine-month hiatus, but there is still no clear pathway to ending the current conflict which started in February 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine.Trump, as of late, has raised eyebrows over his interactions with Putin. On the sidelines of the APEC summit last week, he warmly greeted the Russian leader by referring to him as a “friend.” The remark led to stern criticism from the likes of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.Last month, Trump waived sanctions on Russia to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin in an attempt to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran. The move drew condemnation from European leaders and Republican lawmakers.Russia-Ukraine war intensifies with no clear end in sightRussia on Thursday accused Ukraine of attempting to expand the geographical scope of the conflict into the Mediterranean and Baltic seas, after Kyiv claimed responsibility for an attack on a Russian warship stationed at a port in Libya and another strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that the attacks could “cause concern among coastal states and, most likely, within the North Atlantic alliance as a whole,” according to Russian state media.As tensions escalate, Russia launched fresh strikes on Kyiv overnight into Thursday morning, injuring at least seven people, according to the Ukrainian capital's mayor, Vitali Klitschko. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed carrying out strikes, claiming via a Telegram post that it had targeted Ukrainian military equipment with precision weapons.Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi added that as part of the overnight attacks two foreign ships carrying more than 100,000 tons of grain had been attacked near Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Odessa. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its forces had struck a dry cargo ship with military equipment.In two separate strikes, Ukrainian forces hit an oil terminal refinery deep into Russian territory, and an airfield base in southern Russia.Zelensky on Thursday also said that Russia was planning a major attack on Ukraine’s power grid. “According to intelligence, energy facilities and logistics infrastructure, as well as essential services facilities in cities and communities, will once again be the targets. I expect a report from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry on the results of its communication with our partners regarding the supply of air defenses—interceptors for Patriots and NASAMS [Norwegian Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System] are the key priority,” he said via a social media update. Europe ramps up pressure on RussiaEurope this week unveiled a sweeping new sanctions proposal aimed at further isolating Russia economically and increasing pressure on Moscow to end the war.Leaders of the E.U.’s 27 member states met Thursday in Brussels to discuss the bloc’s long-term budget for 2028-2034 and to address Ukraine’s financial needs for 2027. Ahead of the meeting, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told reporters that Europe "cannot afford cuts to defense funding" and instead needs to invest more in its security. "If you look at what Russia is doing on the eastern border, the eastern border needs protecting, it needs investments and money," he said.Ukraine “probably will face a winter like hell” and so “they must know that Europe has their back, with money and everything we have," he urged.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also insisted that support for Ukraine should continue to be at the forefront of discussions. “We must ensure that Ukraine receives sufficient support in the coming years. That applies both militarily and in humanitarian terms,” he said.Ukraine and its allies have pushed to secure a European seat at the next round of negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations."Europe will be represented by five countries plus the European Union and NATO, and America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation in the negotiations is necessary," Zelensky said last week after attending a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin. Zelensky has since said that Kyiv is “waiting for the American side to set a date for the next meeting.” TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.

clusters.title: ‘Not a Close Case’: Judge Strikes Down Trump Administration’s Targeting of ABC
clusters.neutral_headline: ‘Not a Close Case’: Judge Strikes Down Trump Administration’s Targeting of ABC

items.title: ‘Not a Close Case’: Judge Strikes Down Trump Administration’s Targeting of ABC
items.standfirst: The Federal Communications Commission cannot subject ABC stations to early license review, a federal judge ruled, citing the President’s public statements attacking the network.
items.content: An ABC logo on the side of the network’s building in New York City. —Gary Hershorn—Getty ImagesA federal judge has blocked the Trump Administration’s communications regulator from targeting network ABC, ruling against an early review of the broadcaster’s licenses that critics have claimed is part of the Administration’s attacks on the press.U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., granted ABC’s request for a preliminary injunction against the Federal Communications Commission’s review, saying that the network was likely to succeed on its First Amendment claim. “This is not a close case,” the judge wrote in her Wednesday ruling.The FCC, chaired by President Donald Trump’s appointee Brendan Carr, opened a review of licenses of ABC’s eight local television stations in April following a series of run-ins with the Trump Administration involving the network’s shows. ABC and its parent company Disney sued the Commission in August.President Donald Trump reacts as FCC Chairman Brendan Carr speaks during a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13, 2026. —Kent Nishimura—AFP/Getty Images“Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness,” AliKhan, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, wrote.A spokesperson for ABC News celebrated the decision, calling it “an important victory for the First Amendment.”The FCC said in a statement to the media that the ruling was “wrong on the facts and wrong on the law,” adding: “We will ​continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.” AliKhan’s ruling did not bar the FCC from conducting future reviews.Anna Gomez, the FCC’s lone Democratic commissioner, said in a statement that the ruling “brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an Administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control.”The saga between ABC and the FCC comes as the Trump Administration has launched several legal battles against the American press since his return to the White House almost two years ago. The outcomes have been mixed: a case involving CBS’ 60 Minutes ended in a multimillion-dollar settlement to Trump, while a suit over The Wall Street Journal’s reporting on Trump’s alleged birthday letter to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein was dismissed. Other cases are still pending, including the Associated Press’ federal appeal over White House press access restrictions.But after the FCC injunction, “outlets that Carr has intimidated can breathe a little easier,” Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at non-profit organization Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement, urging others to bring their free speech opponents to court. “The lesson to learn from this ruling is don’t cave to Carr or any other anti-speech bullies in this Administration.”Trump’s gripes with ABCTrump has long antagonized news organizations for their critical coverage of him. In December 2024, just weeks before his inauguration, ABC agreed to contribute $15 million toward Trump’s presidential library, pay $1 million in legal fees, and publish an apology, after Trump sued the network over one of its anchors erroneously saying in March that a jury found Trump civilly liable for raping E. Jean Carroll. Trump was found civilly liable for sexual abuse of Carroll but not for rape.In September last year, ABC late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel used the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk as material for a joke, which elicited criticism from conservatives. Carr then threatened regulatory action against Kimmel, ABC, and Disney. On Sept. 17, 2025, Disney took Kimmel’s show off the air, but it returned to the airwaves after about a week.The Carr-led FCC also took issue with another show on the network, The View, and raised that the daytime talk show should be subject to its “equal-time” requirements. The commission has accused the show of hosting political figures without granting time to their opponents. In February, Carr confirmed that his agency was investigating the show following the appearance of James Talarico, a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate for Texas at the time who would later win in the November midterm elections.In April, President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump bristled at another on-air joke from Kimmel that aired April 23 and called for the late-night show host to be fired. Following their comments, the FCC on April 28 ordered early reviews of the broadcast licenses for eight ABC-owned stations, with the agency saying it was looking into possible alleged violations of the Communications Act of 1934 and the FCC’s rules, including the agency’s prohibition on “unlawful discrimination.” ABC then sued in August, arguing that the Administration had “waged a retaliatory campaign” for “a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts.” It argued that the Commission had not called for a renewal application “ahead of schedule in more than half a century,” nor had it sought “simultaneous early renewal applications from a group of stations commonly owned with a single broadcast network.”The FCC generally reviews broadcast licenses once every eight years, and such reviews are usually staggered instead of all at once. ABC’s licenses were also not due for renewal until 2028 at the earliest.Speaking to the Financial Times in May, Carr acknowledged the rarity of the early review. “It’s probably been 50, 60 years or longer since the FCC has used this tool,” he told the paper, adding: “If you didn’t take us seriously, now you should.”What the ruling saidThroughout the ruling, AliKhan referred to Trump’s and Carr’s public statements and social media posts attacking Disney and ABC. “What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC ‘can keep getting a license’ if it ‘report[s] fake news,’ … has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC’s broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions,” AliKhan wrote, adding that Carr “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders.”AliKhan added that the FCC’s early review for license renewal had a “chilling effect,” including on how the network would book political guests on its shows and how it covers President Trump and related topics.The federal judge also rejected the FCC’s argument against a court intervention since it has not yet rejected the license renewals. “To be sure, Plaintiffs would face even greater injury if the FCC ultimately denied their renewal applications,” AliKhan wrote. “But that does not mean that they are not currently being injured by allegedly being singled out for differential treatment—that is, from facing early license renewal proceedings years in advance of the standard expiration dates as a cudgel to stamp out unfavorable content about President Trump.”
